ai.definition: Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) are a technology that involves creating artificial permeability in hot, dry rocks deep within the Earth's crust to extract geothermal energy. This is achieved by injecting high-pressure fluids into these rocks to create or expand fracture networks, which allows for the extraction of heat and conversion into electricity.
ai.howItWorks: EGS technologies involve drilling wells into hot, dry rock formations typically found at depths between 3-5 kilometers. High-pressure fluid injection is then used to create or enhance existing fractures within these rocks. This process increases the permeability of the rock formation, allowing for the circulation of water through the system. The heated water is extracted from one well and injected back into another, creating a closed-loop system that continuously circulates the fluid to extract heat energy.
ai.problemSolved: EGS addresses the challenge of accessing geothermal resources in areas where natural permeability is insufficient or non-existent, thereby expanding the potential locations for geothermal power generation. It enables baseload power production with consistent and reliable energy output, independent of weather conditions or time of day.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves specialized drilling equipment, high-pressure injection systems, and well completion techniques designed to withstand extreme temperatures and pressures. These components need to be robust enough to function in deep underground environments where traditional materials may degrade quickly.
ai.buildProcess: Building an EGS system requires multiple stages: initial exploration and feasibility studies, drilling of wells, hydraulic fracturing to create permeable pathways, installation of production and injection equipment, and finally, the operational phase where heat is extracted and converted into electricity. This process can take several years from start to finish.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include high initial capital investment for drilling and well completion, specialized equipment, and the complexity of the technology. Additionally, environmental considerations such as potential induced seismicity and water management add to the overall costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: EGS is currently in the early stages of widespread commercial deployment but has significant potential for growth as technologies improve and more projects are developed. The technology is expected to play a crucial role in renewable energy portfolios, particularly in regions with suitable geology.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by country, but there is increasing interest in EGS due to its potential for baseload power generation. Regulations often focus on environmental impact assessments, induced seismicity monitoring, and water management plans. However, specific standards are still being developed as the technology matures.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include concerns about induced seismicity, groundwater contamination, and land subsidence. Technical challenges involve ensuring long-term stability of the reservoirs and maintaining efficient fluid circulation. Economic risks stem from high initial costs and the need for sustained financial investment over the project lifecycle.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable depending on factors such as resource quality, operational efficiency, and local energy market conditions. While EGS projects can provide stable revenue streams due to baseload power generation, they require significant upfront capital and ongoing maintenance investments.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development of EGS will likely focus on improving drilling techniques, reducing environmental impacts, and optimizing reservoir management strategies. Innovations in materials science and fluid chemistry could also enhance the efficiency and longevity of EGS systems.

glossary.def: A form of electricity generation that provides a constant level of supply to meet minimum demand.
Seismic activity triggered by human activities, such as fluid injection or extraction in EGS projects.
A cycle where the same fluid is continuously circulated through a geothermal reservoir without external water sources.

subsystems.name: Injection and production wells
subsystems.role: carry water several kilometres down into hot rock and bring it back up.
parts: deep directional wells with horizontal sections

subsystems.name: Engineered fracture network
subsystems.role: the man-made 'reservoir' — cracks opened in hot, dry rock so water can flow through and pick up heat.

subsystems.name: Surface power plant
parts: binary-cycle (organic Rankine) turbine or flash plant

subsystems.name: Circulation loop
subsystems.role: pumps water down and keeps the loop clean.

subsystems.name: Seismic monitoring
subsystems.role: watches for induced earthquakes while fractures are opened and during operation.

buildSteps.title: Find the hot rock
buildSteps.detail: Geophysical surveys and temperature-gradient wells locate rock that is hot enough at a drillable depth.

buildSteps.title: Drill the injection well
buildSteps.detail: Oil-and-gas rigs drill down and turn horizontal through the hot rock, using hard-wearing PDC bits.

buildSteps.title: Stimulate fractures
buildSteps.detail: Water is pumped in stages at high pressure to open cracks in the rock, with microseismic monitoring throughout.

buildSteps.title: Drill production wells
buildSteps.detail: Second wells are drilled to intersect the fracture zone.

buildSteps.title: Circulate
buildSteps.detail: Cold water goes down the injector, flows through the hot fractures and returns hot up the producers.

buildSteps.title: Generate and reinject
buildSteps.detail: The heat drives a binary-cycle turbine; cooled water is pumped back down in a closed loop.

prerequisites.why: borrowed from shale oil and gas — the main reason EGS became viable.

prerequisites.tech: Fast, cheap drilling in hard, hot rock
prerequisites.why: drilling is most of the cost, and hot granite wears tools out.
earlier projects (Basel in 2006, Pohang in 2017) were halted after felt earthquakes.
electronics and seals must survive conditions that destroy standard gear.

pathway.milestone: first commercial pilots (e.g. Fervo Energy's Project Red in Nevada)
pathway.unlocks: proof that shale-style drilling makes flowing reservoirs.

pathway.milestone: projects in the hundreds of megawatts
pathway.unlocks: cost reductions from drilling many similar wells.

pathway.milestone: superhot rock above about 374 °C, where water goes supercritical
pathway.unlocks: several times more energy per well.

pathway.milestone: geothermal almost anywhere by drilling deep enough
pathway.unlocks: round-the-clock clean power without volcanic geology.
